claim: Animals integrate different senses to facilitate event-detection for navigation in their environment.
source: Animals integrate the different senses to facilitate event-detection for navigation in their environment.
evidence: This is a general statement about animal behavior that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: In vertebrates, the optic tectum (superior colliculus) commands gaze shifts by synaptic integration of different sensory modalities.
source: In vertebrates, the optic tectum (superior colliculus) commands gaze shifts by synaptic integration of different sensory modalities.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to established scientific literature on the optic tectum/superior colliculus function.

claim: Recent works suggest that tectum can elaborate gaze reorientation commands on its own, rather than merely acting as a relay from upstream/forebrain circuits to downstream premotor centers.
source: Recent works suggest that tectum can elaborate gaze reorientation commands on its own, rather than merely acting as a relay from upstream/forebrain circuits to downstream premotor centers.
evidence: This claim references recent scientific literature suggesting a revised understanding of tectal function.

claim: Single tectal neurons receive converging visual and electrosensory inputs in the lamprey.
source: Single tectal neurons receive converging visual and electrosensory inputs, as investigated in the lamprey - a phylogenetically conserved vertebrate.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: When visual and electrosensory inputs overlap in space and time, response enhancement of output neurons occurs locally in the tectum.
source: When these two sensory inputs overlap in space and time, response enhancement of output neurons occurs locally in the tectum, whereas surrounding areas and temporally misaligned inputs are inhibited.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Surrounding areas and temporally misaligned inputs are inhibited during multisensory integration.
source: When these two sensory inputs overlap in space and time, response enhancement of output neurons occurs locally in the tectum, whereas surrounding areas and temporally misaligned inputs are inhibited.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Retinal and electrosensory afferents elicit local monosynaptic excitation in tectal neurons.
source: Retinal and electrosensory afferents elicit local monosynaptic excitation, quickly followed by inhibition via recruitment of GABAergic interneurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by whole-cell recording data.

claim: Monosynaptic excitation is quickly followed by inhibition via recruitment of GABAergic interneurons.
source: Retinal and electrosensory afferents elicit local monosynaptic excitation, quickly followed by inhibition via recruitment of GABAergic interneurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electrophysiological recordings and pharmacological experiments.

claim: Multisensory inputs can regulate event-detection within tectum through local inhibition without forebrain control.
source: Multisensory inputs can thus regulate event-detection within tectum through local inhibition without forebrain control.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data showing tectal circuits can perform multisensory computations independently.

claim: The optic tectum (superior colliculus in mammals) has a distinct role in orienting behavior and control of orienting and avoidance gaze movements.
source: The optic tectum (superior colliculus in mammals), has received particular attention for its distinct role in orienting behavior, i.e. the control of orienting and avoidance gaze movements (Dean et al., 1989; Moschovakis et al., 1996; Basso and Wurtz, 1997; Sparks, 2002)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The optic tectum integrates different sensory modalities including vision, auditory and electroreception.
source: through the integration of different sensory modalities (which are species-dependent) like vision, auditory and electroreception (Bodznick and Northcutt, 1981; Meredith and Stein, 1986; Wallace et al., 1996, Gingras et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Combining multiple sensory inputs has been proposed to increase the reliability of event detection in the environment.
source: Although combining multiple sensory inputs has been proposed to increase the reliability of event detection in the environment (Ernst and Banks, 2002; Fetsch et al., 2009), little is known about the neural mechanisms underlying this integration.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Little is known about the neural mechanisms underlying multisensory integration.
source: Although combining multiple sensory inputs has been proposed to increase the reliability of event detection in the environment (Ernst and Banks, 2002; Fetsch et al., 2009), little is known about the neural mechanisms underlying this integration.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in scientific knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Extracellular activity correlated to gaze shift execution increases with spatiotemporally congruent cues from two senses.
source: In particular, extracellular activity correlated to gaze shift execution would increase with spatiotemporally congruent cues from two senses or decrease with spatially disparate and/or temporally asynchronous cues (Meredith et al., 1987; Meredith and Stein, 1996; Kadunce et al., 1997; Recanzone, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Extracellular activity correlated to gaze shift execution decreases with spatially disparate and/or temporally asynchronous cues.
source: In particular, extracellular activity correlated to gaze shift execution would increase with spatiotemporally congruent cues from two senses or decrease with spatially disparate and/or temporally asynchronous cues (Meredith et al., 1987; Meredith and Stein, 1996; Kadunce et al., 1997; Recanzone, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Computational models of multisensory integration have proposed the existence of an inhibitory mechanism to account for multisensory effects.
source: Conceptual and computational models of multisensory integration have proposed the existence of an inhibitory mechanism to account for these effects (Rowland et al., 2007; Alvarado et al., 2008; Ursino et al., 2009; Ohshiro et al., 2011; Miller et al., 2015), although they have so far remained hypothetical.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior computational modeling studies.

claim: The inhibitory mechanisms proposed by computational models have remained hypothetical.
source: Conceptual and computational models of multisensory integration have proposed the existence of an inhibitory mechanism to account for these effects (Rowland et al., 2007; Alvarado et al., 2008; Ursino et al., 2009; Ohshiro et al., 2011; Miller et al., 2015), although they have so far remained hypothetical.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in empirical validation of theoretical models.

claim: Vision and electroreception are spatial senses used to localize predators and prey in many vertebrates.
source: In many vertebrates, vision and electroreception are the spatial senses that are used to localize predators and prey in their immediate environment
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about vertebrate sensory systems.

claim: These sensory modalities are represented within the optic tectum and are used for orienting and avoidance behaviors in vertebrates extending from lampreys to primates.
source: These modalities are represented within the optic tectum and are used for orienting and avoidance behaviors (Hartline et al., 1978; Semm and Demaine, 1986; Valentine and Moss, 1997) in vertebrates extending from lampreys to primates (Wurtz and Albano, 1980; Nieuwenhuys and Nicholson, 1998; Saitoh et al., 2007; Jones et al., 2009; Asteriti et al., 2015; Kardamakis et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Site-specific stimulation across the deep layer of the optic tectum gives rise to eye-head gaze shifts of given amplitude and direction in the lamprey.
source: We have previously shown in the lamprey that site-specific stimulation across the deep layer of the optic tectum gives rise to eye-head gaze shifts of given amplitude and direction, thus, showing the existence of a motor map (Saitoh et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement refers to prior work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: Visual and electroreceptive inputs are integrated in the same deep layer neurons of the optic tectum.
source: We now show that visual and electroreceptive inputs are integrated in the same deep layer neurons of the optic tectum, which provide the output to different brainstem centers.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Deep layer neurons of the optic tectum provide output to different brainstem centers.
source: We now show that visual and electroreceptive inputs are integrated in the same deep layer neurons of the optic tectum, which provide the output to different brainstem centers.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Video 1 and Figure 1.

claim: Projecting output neurons and local interneurons receive monosynaptic excitatory input from both sensory afferent pathways.
source: Projecting output neurons, as well as local interneurons, receive monosynaptic excitatory input from both sensory afferent pathways and also disynaptic inhibition triggered by the same afferents.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Projecting output neurons and local interneurons receive disynaptic inhibition triggered by the same afferents.
source: Projecting output neurons, as well as local interneurons, receive monosynaptic excitatory input from both sensory afferent pathways and also disynaptic inhibition triggered by the same afferents.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electrophysiological recordings and pharmacological experiments.

claim: When two signals are activated from the same point in space, both excitation and inhibition occur, whereas signals from surrounding areas provide only inhibition.
source: This applies if the two signals are activated from the same point in space, whereas signals from surrounding areas provide only inhibition (Kardamakis et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work and data in the current study.

claim: The membrane properties of tectal output neurons ensure the temporal integration of bimodally triggered excitatory and inhibitory currents.
source: The membrane properties of the tectal output neurons ensure the temporal integration of bimodally triggered excitatory and inhibitory currents.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by whole-cell recording data and conductance analysis.

claim: The organization of the optic tectum is highly conserved across vertebrates.
source: Due to the highly conserved organization of the optic tectum (Nieuwenhuys and Nicholson, 1998; Saitoh et al., 2007; Jones et al., 2009; Asteriti et al., 2015; Kardamakis et al., 2015), we anticipate that the mechanisms of integration of two senses on single output neurons, as demonstrated here, may also apply to other vertebrates.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to comparative neuroanatomy studies.

claim: The mechanisms of integration of two senses on single output neurons demonstrated in lamprey may also apply to other vertebrates.
source: Due to the highly conserved organization of the optic tectum (Nieuwenhuys and Nicholson, 1998; Saitoh et al., 2007; Jones et al., 2009; Asteriti et al., 2015; Kardamakis et al., 2015), we anticipate that the mechanisms of integration of two senses on single output neurons, as demonstrated here, may also apply to other vertebrates.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on comparative anatomy and the current findings.

claim: Tectal efferents arise from neurons in the deep layer and project to the brainstem.
source: Tectal efferents arise from neurons in the deep layer (DL) and project to the brainstem, where they make direct synaptic contacts onto the somata of reticulospinal (RS) neurons in the middle rhombencephalic reticulospinal nucleus (MRRN).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Video 1.

claim: Tectal efferents make direct synaptic contacts onto the somata of reticulospinal neurons in the middle rhombencephalic reticulospinal nucleus.
source: Tectal efferents arise from neurons in the deep layer (DL) and project to the brainstem, where they make direct synaptic contacts onto the somata of reticulospinal (RS) neurons in the middle rhombencephalic reticulospinal nucleus (MRRN).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Video 1.

claim: Projecting neurons in the deep layer of the optic tectum control gaze movements.
source: These projecting neurons in the deep layer of the optic tectum (or superior colliculus) control gaze movements (Sparks, 2002; Robertson et al., 2006, Saitoh et al., 2007; Jones et al., 2009; Kardamakis et al., 2015)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Visual and electrosensory modalities have spatially segregated termination zones with minimal overlap in the optic tectum.
source: By injecting two different tracers into the contralateral optic nerve and the contralateral octavolateral area (Figure 1A-i), we revealed that the two sensory modalities have spatially segregated termination zones with minimal overlap (retina in red, octavolateral in green; n = 3, Figure 1A-ii).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Retinal input targets the superficial layer of the optic tectum.
source: Retinal input targets the superficial layer, while electroreceptive afferents project to the intermediate layer.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1A-ii.

claim: Electroreceptive afferents project to the intermediate layer of the optic tectum.
source: Retinal input targets the superficial layer, while electroreceptive afferents project to the intermediate layer.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1A-ii.

claim: Deep layer neurons have dendritic arbors extending through the intermediate and into the superficial layers.
source: The deep layer (DL, visible with the Nissl stain; in blue) contains neurons that have dendritic arbors extending through the intermediate and into the superficial layers (Figure 1A-iii), as revealed by intracellular staining of output neurons that were prelabeled following retrograde tracer injections into the MRRN.
evidence: This is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 1A-iii.

claim: Deep layer output neurons exhibit the optimal morphological structure to support sampling of layer-specific inputs carrying visual and electrosensory information.
source: Effectively, they exhibit the optimal morphological structure to support sampling of layer-specific inputs carrying visual and electrosensory information.
evidence: This is an inference based on the morphological data showing dendritic arbors spanning multiple layers.

claim: When visual and electrosensory inputs were delivered in an overlapping temporal sequence, there was a marked enhancement of deep layer neural activity.
source: When the two sensory inputs were delivered in an overlapping temporal sequence, there was a marked enhancement of deep layer neural activity (Figure 1C-iii, control; n = 6).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by extracellular recording data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: To achieve enhancement, the two stimuli had to be delivered to the same parts of the visual and electroreceptive fields.
source: To achieve an enhancement, the two stimuli had to be delivered to the same parts of the visual and electroreceptive fields, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Unisensory inputs generated up to ~55% of the maximal bimodal response across the entire stimulus range.
source: Unisensory inputs generated up to ~55% of the maximal bimodal response across the entire stimulus range.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: During bimodal activation, the combined response significantly exceeded the unimodal responses.
source: During bimodal activation, the combined response significantly exceeded the unimodal responses (visual-bimodal: p<0.01; electrosensory-bimodal: p<0.001 between 100–1000 μs; Figure 1D, black control trace).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: On-receptive field visual responses in tectal output layer neurons can be suppressed by the presence of multiple visual stimuli located at disparate positions in the visual field.
source: Recently, we have shown how on-receptive field visual responses in tectal output layer neurons can be suppressed, via the local inhibitory system, by the presence of multiple visual stimuli located at disparate positions in the visual field (Kardamakis et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement refers to prior work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: Unisensory response suppression can be achieved by using multiple stimuli of different sensory modalities.
source: We now show that this unisensory response suppression can also be achieved by using multiple stimuli of different sensory modalities (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: An average response reduction of ~75% was observed during spatially misaligned cross-modal sensory stimulation.
source: An average response reduction of ~75% was observed during spatially misaligned cross-modal sensory stimulation (Figure 2C; red for electrosensory and black for bimodal stimulation; n = 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Microinjection of gabazine resulted in a marked increase in the magnitude of the response during drug application.
source: To evaluate the role of local inhibition, we microinjected the GABAA-receptor antagonist gabazine (10 μM) in the area of the recording site (Figure 1B). We observed a marked increase in the magnitude of the response during drug application (Figure 1C, bottom traces).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by pharmacological manipulation and extracellular recording data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Without inhibition, neurons in the deep layer became irresponsive to following incoming stimuli for a refractory period that exceeded 30 s.
source: Without inhibition, neurons in the deep layer became irresponsive to the following incoming stimuli for a refractory period that exceeded 30 s (n = 6).
evidence: This is a primary finding from pharmacological experiments.

claim: When gabazine was microinjected, the responses increased by approximately 80–100% compared to their original magnitude throughout the stimulus durations.
source: When gabazine was microinjected (Figure 1C,D), the responses increased by approximately 80–100% compared to their original magnitude throughout the stimulus durations (for visual: 85.5 ± 13.7%; electrosensory: 97.4 ± 14.4%; for bimodal: 82.4 ± 13.0, Means ± SD; n = 13)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: After gabazine application, the relationship between unimodal and bimodal responses quickly deteriorated with visual inputs dominating bimodal activation.
source: At the same time, the relationship between unimodal and bimodal responses quickly deteriorated (no significant differences) with visual inputs dominating bimodal activation.
evidence: This is a finding from pharmacological experiments and statistical analysis.

claim: Tectal inhibition is critical to ensure response enhancement and a stable relationship between response amplitudes to unimodal inputs.
source: Our data thus suggest that tectal inhibition is critical to ensure response enhancement and a stable relationship between response amplitudes to unimodal inputs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pharmacological experiments showing loss of enhancement after gabazine application.

claim: Bimodal activation resulted in a higher spiking probability of single stimulus-locked action potentials compared to unimodal stimulation.
source: Bimodal activation resulted in a higher spiking probability of single stimulus-locked action potentials (statistical differences of p<0.001).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell-attached recording data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Reducing stimulation threshold by 30% would elicit a suprathreshold response only when both pathways were engaged.
source: Reducing T by 30% (0.7xT) would elicit a suprathreshold response only when both pathways were engaged (Figure 3C, middle panel).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell-attached recording data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The combined action of weaker stimuli leading to stronger bimodal responses is a key feature underlying multisensory integration.
source: This combined action of weaker stimuli leading to stronger bimodal responses is a key feature underlying multisensory integration.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Enhancement is completely lost in the absence of local GABAergic inhibition.
source: This enhancement is completely lost in the absence of local GABAergic inhibition, where output neurons rapidly fired multiple action potentials even in response to normally ineffective stimuli as in the case of 0.7xT (Figure 3C, right panel; see also Figure 1C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Tectal output cells have long membrane time constants (98.8 ± 11.5 ms, n = 32).
source: Notably, these cells have long membrane time constants (98.8 ± 11.5 ms, n = 32; see Materials and methods) due to their high input resistance (0.95 ± 0.24 GOhm, n = 32).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from whole-cell recording experiments.

claim: Tectal output cells have high input resistance (0.95 ± 0.24 GOhm, n = 32).
source: Notably, these cells have long membrane time constants (98.8 ± 11.5 ms, n = 32; see Materials and methods) due to their high input resistance (0.95 ± 0.24 GOhm, n = 32).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from whole-cell recording experiments.

claim: The long membrane time constant facilitates the temporal summation of excitatory currents.
source: This property facilitates the temporal summation of excitatory currents and ensures that distal visual inputs (in superficial layer) and more proximal electrosensory inputs (in intermediate layer) will yield functionally similar responses (i.e. amplitude and temporal characteristics) at the final integration site in the soma (in the deep layer; see Figure 1C, top traces).
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured membrane properties and their functional implications.

claim: Output neurons discharge action potentials with a regular firing pattern in response to stepwise increases of applied current.
source: Furthermore, output neurons also discharge action potentials with a regular firing pattern in response to stepwise increases of applied current, and display a continuous and linear frequency-current relationship in the lower range of current injections (Figure 4A-iii; slope: 0.53 ± 0.05 spikes/pA, n = 32).
evidence: This is a primary finding from whole-cell recording experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Output neurons have a linear input-output relationship across a wide range of membrane potentials (−120 to −20 mV).
source: All neurons that were recorded had a linear input-output relationship across a wide range of membrane potentials (−120 to −20 mV; Figure 4A-iv)
evidence: This is a primary finding from whole-cell recording experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Output neurons smoothly encode the strength of similar sensory inputs into output firing frequency.
source: and would, thus, smoothly encode the strength of similar sensory inputs into output firing frequency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the linear input-output relationship.

claim: Excitatory postsynaptic potentials were evoked onto the same output neurons by stimulation of retinal and octavolateral afferent pathways.
source: We found that excitatory postsynaptic potentials were evoked onto the same output neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding from whole-cell recording experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A concurrent inhibitory postsynaptic potential was revealed when the membrane potential was held at −20 mV.
source: A concurrent inhibitory postsynaptic potential was also revealed when the membrane potential was held at −20 mV (upper range of the linear domain of their V-I curve) in current clamp mode.
evidence: This is a primary finding from whole-cell recording experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The inhibition is feedforward and is produced mainly disynaptically by projections of tectal interneurons onto output neurons.
source: This inhibition is feedforward and is produced mainly disynaptically by projections of tectal interneurons onto output neurons (Kardamakis et al., 2015; see below).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work and data in the current study.

claim: Output neurons reach threshold more reliably and faster when both sensory modalities are present.
source: Consistent with extracellular (Figure 1C) and cell-attached recordings (Figure 3A), the output neurons reach threshold more reliably and faster when both sensory modalities are present (black trace in Figure 4C; resting at −69 mV; top traces)
evidence: This is a primary finding from whole-cell recording experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The inhibition persisted during both unimodal and bimodal stimulation.
source: Notably, the inhibition persisted not only during unimodal but also during bimodal stimulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from whole-cell recording experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The membrane properties of output neurons are able to support the smooth integration of sensory-evoked excitation coupled to triggered inhibition.
source: Together, these data indicate that the membrane properties of output neurons are able to support the smooth integration of sensory-evoked excitation coupled to triggered inhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological characterization of output neurons.

claim: Whole-cell current recordings began with a direct excitatory current that was followed ~5–10 ms later by an intense inhibitory current.
source: Whole-cell current recordings (retinal are blue traces; octavolateral are red traces) began with a direct excitatory current that was followed ~5–10 ms later by an intense inhibitory current (see also Kardamakis et al., 2015)
evidence: This is a primary finding from voltage-clamp experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: When co-stimulating both afferent pathways, excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic current amplitudes increased in direct correspondence to the unimodal-evoked responses.
source: When co-stimulating both afferent pathways, excitatory postsynaptic current and inhibitory postsynaptic current amplitudes increased in direct correspondence to the unimodal-evoked responses (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from voltage-clamp experiments shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: The statistical difference in the magnitude of evoked EPSC and IPSC currents by bimodal and visual or electroreceptive afferent stimulation was significant.
source: On a trial-to-trial basis, the statistical difference in the magnitude of evoked EPSC and IPSC currents by bimodal and visual or electroreceptive afferent stimulation was significant (visual-bimodal: p=0.008; electrosensory-bimodal: p=0.006; one-way ANOVA)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from voltage-clamp experiments.

claim: No statistical significance was detected when comparing the mean differences between the sum of unisensory-evoked and bimodal-evoked currents.
source: Notably, no statistical significance (p=0.85 for EPSCs and p=0.92 for IPSCs) was detected when comparing the mean differences between the sum of unisensory-evoked and bimodal-evoked currents (Figure 5B; EPSCs, visual: 28.63 ± 5.6 pA, electrosensory: 28.4 ± 5.85 pA, both: 56.27 ± 9.11, n = 12; IPSCs, visual: 24.04 ± 6.15 pA, electrosensory: 33.7 ± 14.82 pA, both: 55.22 ± 15.79 pA, n = 7).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from voltage-clamp experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Output neurons are able to temporally integrate the synaptic currents evoked by individual unisensory inputs to generate an enhanced bimodal product.
source: As predicted by their membrane properties, output neurons are able to temporally integrate the synaptic currents evoked by individual unisensory inputs summate to generate an enhanced bimodal product.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the voltage-clamp experiments and membrane property characterization.

claim: Both EPSPs and IPSPs peak constant values after a brief transient phase during repetitive stimulation.
source: After a brief transient phase (usually after three pulses), both EPSPs and IPSPs peak constant values during further repetitive stimulation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from current-clamp experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Bimodal stimulation resulted in larger EPSPs compared to unisensory stimulation.
source: Compared to unisensory stimulation, bimodal stimulation resulted not only in larger EPSPs (visual-bimodal: p=0.0001; electrosensory-bimodal; p=0.006; visual: 12.8 ± 1.4 mV, electrosensory: 10.5 ± 0.9 mV, bimodal: 16.4 ± 1.5 mV, n = 24)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from current-clamp experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Bimodal stimulation resulted in larger IPSPs compared to unisensory stimulation.
source: but also in larger IPSPs (visual-bimodal: p=0.05; electrosensory-bimodal; p=0.02; visual: 11.7 ± 1.4 mV, electrosensory: 10.2 ± 1.2 mV, bimodal: 13.9 ± 1.2 mV, n = 24; Figure 5D)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from current-clamp experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The quick opposing action of feedforward inhibition curtails the temporal window that allows output neurons to integrate excitatory inputs.
source: The quick opposing action of feedforward inhibition curtails the temporal window that allows output neurons to integrate excitatory inputs, thus, restraining the impact that excitation has on membrane potential deflection.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings on the timing of excitation and inhibition.

claim: When bimodal inputs are used, excitatory currents summate and increase the resultant EPSP amplitude but are quickly quenched by a stronger amount of inhibition.
source: When bimodal inputs are used, excitatory currents summate and increase the resultant EPSP amplitude (Figure 5C,D) but are quickly quenched by an also stronger amount of inhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current-clamp experiments shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The reversal potentials for visual, electrosensory and bimodal inputs are near the action potential threshold.
source: Strikingly, these values were observed for the corresponding reversal potentials, which were −48.2 ± 2.7 mV for visual inputs, −50.4 ± 2.2 mV for electrosensory and −48.2 ± 2.4 mV for combined inputs. These values are near the action potential threshold (−43.7 ± 1.0 mV, n = 10; Figure 6A, bottom).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from conductance analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: When the total synaptic conductance is at a maximum, the reversal potential target values are relatively invariant, despite the additional excitatory current when switching from unimodal to bimodal input.
source: When the total synaptic conductance is at a maximum, the reversal potential target values that are relatively invariant, despite the additional excitatory current when switching from unimodal to bimodal input.
evidence: This is a primary finding from conductance analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The latency between the onset of excitation and inhibition is time-locked for both unimodal and bimodal inputs.
source: The latency between the onset of excitation and inhibition is time-locked (Figure 6C) for both unimodal and bimodal inputs, as well as the latency between their peaks.
evidence: This is a primary finding from conductance analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The latency between the onset of Gi and Ge was between 5–10 ms.
source: The latency between the onset of Gi and Ge was between 5–10 ms (n = 10; see arrows in Figure 6C, and Kardamakis et al. [2015])
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from conductance analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The 5-10 ms time lag provides a temporal window of opportunity for output neurons to integrate independent excitatory inputs from each sensory modality.
source: thus, providing a temporal window of opportunity for output neurons to integrate independent excitatory inputs from each sensory modality.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the timing measurements.

claim: This time lag is sufficient for transient stimuli to efficiently summate inputs towards spike threshold before the onset of the inhibition.
source: This time lag is sufficient for transient stimuli to efficiently summate inputs towards spike threshold before the onset of the inhibition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the timing measurements.

claim: The quenching effect of feedforward inhibition can account for the mismatch between the evoked EPSP amplitudes to their underlying excitatory conductances during bimodal stimulation.
source: The quenching effect of this feedforward inhibition can account for the mismatch between the evoked EPSP amplitudes to their underlying excitatory conductances during bimodal stimulation, i.e. the subadditive effect of combining both sensory inputs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the relationship between conductances and membrane potentials.

claim: The summating effect observed in the synaptic current measurements obtained in voltage clamp is reflected in Ge and Gi.
source: Furthermore, the summating effect observed in the synaptic current measurements obtained in voltage clamp (Figure 5A) is also reflected in Ge and Gi (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a comparison between voltage-clamp and conductance analysis results.

claim: Non-linearities in the form of strong voltage-dependent conductances or shunting inhibition are not likely to play a significant role in the gain regulation of responses in output neurons during multisensory integration.
source: This close agreement suggests that non-linearities in the form of strong voltage-dependent conductances or shunting inhibition are not likely to play a significant role in the gain regulation of responses in output neurons during multisensory integration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the agreement between voltage-clamp and conductance analysis.

claim: The maximal response was obtained when the onset of both sensory-evoked EPSPs was aligned so that excitation would be in-phase.
source: The maximal response was obtained when the onset of both sensory-evoked EPSPs was aligned so that excitation would be in-phase, i.e. latency of 0 ms (Figure 7A, left & 6B, black trace)
evidence: This is a primary finding from temporal offset experiments shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Amplitude reduction occurred when afferent stimulation onsets were temporally misaligned using an offset from 5 to 50 ms.
source: whereas amplitude reduction occurred when afferent stimulation onsets were temporally misaligned using an offset from 5 to 50 ms.
evidence: This is a primary finding from temporal offset experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: A maximal attenuation of 15% was achieved with a 5–10 ms latency, matching the maximum peak of inhibition.
source: A maximal attenuation of 15% was achieved with a 5–10 ms latency (see also Figure 7B, orange trace), matching the maximum peak of inhibition
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from temporal offset experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The sequence of sensory modality inputs did not have a differential impact on the attenuation level.
source: Thus, the sequence of sensory modality inputs did not have a differential impact on the attenuation level.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the temporal offset experiments.

claim: The timing of sensory-evoked inhibitory events regulates the responsiveness of output neurons.
source: Taken together, the timing of sensory-evoked inhibitory events regulates the responsiveness of output neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the temporal offset experiments.

claim: GABAergic interneurons are strategically located within the stratum opticum at the interface between the superficial and intermediate layers.
source: As seen in Figure 8A-i,ii, GABAergic interneurons are strategically located within the stratum opticum - at the interface between the superficial and intermediate layers (Isa et al., 1998; Del Bene et al., 2010; Kardamakis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 8A and citations to prior work.

claim: Microstimulation of tectal interneurons elicits monosynaptic inhibition onto output neurons in the presence of glutamate blockade.
source: Previously, we have shown that microstimulation of this population of tectal interneurons elicits monosynaptic inhibition onto output neurons in the presence of glutamate blockade (2 mM Kynurenic acid) to eliminate excitatory transmission (see Figure 2 in Kardamakis et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement refers to prior work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: EPSPs were evoked in tectal interneurons after electrosensory and visual stimulation.
source: EPSPs were evoked (Figure 8B) after a train of stimuli (at 10 Hz) in cells held at −65 mV in current-clamp, both after electrosensory (Figure 8B–i) and visual stimulation (Figure 8B-ii)
evidence: This is a primary finding from whole-cell recordings of interneurons shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The same pool of interneurons is activated by both sensory modalities.
source: showing that the same pool of interneurons is activated by both sensory modalities.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the recording data showing both visual and electrosensory responses in the same interneurons.

claim: Sensory stimulation evoked both excitation and prominent inhibition in tectal interneurons.
source: Remarkably, sensory stimulation not only evoked excitation (EPSPs, visual: 8.6 ± 1.5 mV, electrosensory: 5.6 ± 0.8 mV, n = 8), but also a prominent inhibition (when holding at −45 mV; IPSPs, visual: 9.8 ± 1.6 mV, electrosensory: 9.8 ± 1.7 mV, n = 8).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from whole-cell recordings of interneurons.

claim: Tectal interneurons have a strikingly different morphology compared to output neurons.
source: In addition, these interneurons have a strikingly different morphology (Figure 8C) compared to that of output neurons (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by morphological reconstructions shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Tectal interneurons have broad dendritic arbor extending in all planes over around 200 µm.
source: Figure 8C illustrates six interneurons that have broad dendritic arbor extending in all planes (over around 200 µm), and also bridge the layers of retinal and electroreceptive fiber termination (as shown in Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by morphological reconstructions shown in Figure 8C.

claim: In half of the stained interneurons, long range axonal projections were visible.
source: In half of the neurons that were stained (3/6), it was possible to also see long range axonal projections, as required for the lateral inhibition.
evidence: This is a finding from morphological analysis of stained interneurons.

claim: Action potentials time-locked to the stimulus were recorded during on-receptive field activation of tectal interneurons.
source: As with tectal output neurons, action potentials time-locked to the stimulus were recorded during on-receptive field activation, but disappeared usually after the second pulse (in 5 out of 7 neurons) due to synaptic depression.
evidence: This is a primary finding from cell-attached recordings of interneurons shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Visually-evoked responses in tectal interneurons showed synaptic excitation and inhibition.
source: A representative example of the interplay between visually-evoked synaptic excitation and inhibition in tectal interneurons can be seen when entering whole-cell configuration (Figure 9B) with subthreshold EPSPs (red trace) accompanied by inhibitory postsynaptic potentials visible when depolarizing near threshold (~ −45 mV) with positive somatic current injections (blue trace).
evidence: This is a primary finding from whole-cell recordings of interneurons shown in Figure 9B.

claim: All interneurons recorded received excitation from usually one main quadrant and in some cases from neighboring ones.
source: All interneurons that were recorded received excitation from usually one main quadrant and in some cases (6 out of 13) they also received from neighboring ones.
evidence: This is a finding from systematic mapping of receptive fields in interneurons.

claim: Interneurons displayed a range of variability in their inhibitory responses, subdivided into three provisional groups.
source: Their inhibitory responses, however, displayed a range of variability by which we subdivided into three provisional groups: (a) local excitation and local inhibition (Figure 9E), (b) local excitation and no inhibition (Figure 9F) and (c) local excitation and global inhibition (Figure 9G).
evidence: This is a classification based on systematic characterization of interneuron responses shown in Figure 9E-G.

claim: The spatiotopic arrangement of excitatory components in interneurons is critical for the feedforward inhibition onto tectal output neurons.
source: Despite the variable nature of visually-evoked synaptic inhibition onto tectal interneurons, the spatiotopic arrangement of their excitatory components is critical for the feedforward inhibition onto tectal output neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the receptive field mapping experiments.

claim: Gaze controlling output neurons in the deep layer of the lamprey optic tectum receive visual input from the retina and electroreceptive input from octavolateral afferents.
source: This study relies on the fact that gaze controlling output neurons in the deep layer of the lamprey optic tectum (a) receive visual input from the retina and electroreceptive input from octavolateral afferents
evidence: This is a summary of key findings from the study.

claim: Gaze controlling output neurons are excitatory and target the reticulospinal system within the brainstem that control gaze movements.
source: (b) are excitatory and target the reticulospinal system within the brainstem that control gaze movements (Video 1; see also Saitoh et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data and citation to prior work.

claim: Upon entering the optic tectum, afferents from the retina and octavolateral area contact monosynaptically the same output neurons and inhibitory interneurons.
source: Upon entering the optic tectum, afferents arising from both the retina and the octavolateral area, contact monosynaptically the same output neurons, as well as inhibitory interneurons (GABAergic cells; Figure 10)
evidence: This is a primary finding summarized in the schematic shown in Figure 10.

claim: GABAergic interneurons inhibit output neurons across the tectal map of space.
source: which in turn inhibit output neurons across the tectal map of space.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study.

claim: The disynaptic circuit is able to integrate excitation from different sensory stimuli and feedforward inhibition via interneurons, with spatial and temporal correspondence, to control gaze movements.
source: This disynaptic circuit is able to integrate excitation from different sensory stimuli and feedforward inhibition via interneurons, with spatial and temporal correspondence, to control gaze movements.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's findings.

claim: The tectal GABAergic system regulates the incoming excitatory sensory flow to deep layer output neurons and controls their response profile to stimuli of different modalities.
source: The tectal GABAergic system regulates the incoming excitatory sensory flow to deep layer output neurons and controls their response profile to stimuli of different modalities.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pharmacological and electrophysiological experiments.

claim: The GABAergic system is responsible for the suppression of stimuli with spatial and temporal offsets.
source: It is responsible for the suppression of stimuli with spatial and temporal offsets.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spatial and temporal offset experiments.

claim: On-receptive field retinal stimuli result in local excitation followed by feedforward inhibition, while off-field retinal stimulation yields only lateral inhibition.
source: Recently, we have shown that on-receptive field retinal stimuli result in local excitation followed by feedforward inhibition, while off-field retinal stimulation yields only lateral inhibition, which is widespread (Kardamakis et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement refers to prior work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: Local inhibition can act independently for generating stimulus selection.
source: While this local inhibition can act independently for generating stimulus selection
evidence: This is a conclusion from the current study showing tectal circuits can operate independently.

claim: Exogenous sources have been suggested to be required for generating global inhibition via GABAergic neurons in the isthmic nucleus.
source: it has also been suggested that exogenous sources are required for generating global inhibition via GABAergic neurons in the isthmic nucleus (Mysore and Knudsen, 2013).
evidence: This statement refers to prior work by other researchers, supported by citation.

claim: Inhibition hard-wired in the optic tectum via interneurons is essential for multisensory stimulus selection.
source: Here, we show that inhibition hard-wired in the optic tectum via interneurons, that are activated from both retinal and electroreceptive afferents in the same way as the output neurons, is essential for multisensory stimulus selection.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: The two types of sensory inputs evoke excitation in tectal interneurons and also trigger recurrent inhibition.
source: Notably, the two types of sensory inputs not only evoke excitation in tectal interneurons, but also trigger recurrent inhibition.
evidence: This is a primary finding from whole-cell recordings of interneurons.

claim: Spatiotopic organization in the optic tectum is columnar, with output neurons and interneurons receiving retinal excitation from the same quadrant.
source: Our results suggest that spatiotopic organization in the optic tectum is columnar, with output neurons and interneurons receiving retinal excitation from the same quadrant, as suggested by their morphological features and the fact that the excitation is retinotopically arranged.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the morphological and functional data.

claim: Sensory inputs provide monosynaptic drive to the deep layer output cells and to superficial layer interneurons.
source: Sensory inputs provide monosynaptic drive to the deep layer output cells and to superficial layer interneurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the electrophysiological experiments.

claim: Superficial layer interneurons provide local and long-range inhibitory projections, allowing for spatial sensory discrimination.
source: The latter, in turn, provide local and long-range inhibitory projections, therefore allowing for spatial sensory discrimination.
evidence: This is supported by morphological data and functional experiments.

claim: Responses in on-field regions of tectum to electrosensory stimulation undergo drastic reduction when delivering visual stimuli to other receptive fields.
source: Consistent with bimodal suppression in mammals (Meredith and Stein, 1996; Kadunce et al., 1997), responses in on-field regions of tectum to electrosensory stimulation undergo a drastic reduction when delivering visual stimuli to other receptive fields of the tectal map.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the cross-modal suppression experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Electrosensory maps in the lamprey tectum may not be as refined as the visual ones.
source: One possibility is that electrosensory maps in the lamprey tectum are not as refined as the visual ones, and therefore inhibition is less effective suppressing off-regions.
evidence: This is speculation to explain the asymmetry in cross-modal suppression.

claim: Electrosensory receptive fields in elasmobranchs tectum are much larger than the visual ones.
source: In this sense, it has been shown that electrosensory receptive fields in elasmobranchs tectum are much larger than the visual ones (Bodznick, 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Inhibitory connections embedded within the tectal circuit can account for how normally effective stimuli can be attenuated by the presence of bimodal stimuli when they are spatial and/or temporally misaligned.
source: Consistent with our previous findings, these data suggest that inhibitory connections embedded within the tectal circuit can account for how normally effective stimuli can be attenuated by the presence of bimodal stimuli when they are spatial and/or temporally misaligned.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The GABAergic system allows for response enhancement during bimodal integration.
source: Despite the powerful action of the GABAergic system, it does allow for response enhancement during bimodal integration.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experiments showing enhancement despite inhibition.

claim: Output neurons yield responses of matching amplitudes to both types of sensory inputs, without any apparent domination by a particular modality.
source: The output neurons yield responses of matching amplitudes to both types of sensory inputs, without any apparent domination by a particular modality.
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological experiments.

claim: Two overlapping stimuli from two modalities produce a stronger response than when only one modality is present.
source: Two overlapping (in space and time) stimuli from these two modalities will produce a stronger response, than when only one modality is present.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the multisensory integration experiments.

claim: Two sensory modalities that provide stimuli spatially and temporally aligned are most likely related to the same external event.
source: As a rule, two sensory modalities that provide stimuli spatially and temporally aligned are most likely related to the same external event.
evidence: This is a general principle about sensory integration based on ecological considerations.

claim: Response enhancement caused by the integration of two senses gives rise to higher event detection reliability.
source: In this manner, the response enhancement caused by the integration of two senses gives rise to higher event detection reliability.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of multisensory enhancement.

claim: Bimodal inputs increase the amount of depolarization in output neurons and increase the probability of evoking an action potential.
source: When this occurs, bimodal inputs are able to increase the amount of depolarization in output neurons and increase the probability of evoking an action potential, and therefore, to activate their downstream targets and elicit a motor response.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the electrophysiological experiments.

claim: Tectal inhibition continuously resets active areas to enable constant monitoring of information flow from the environment.
source: Tectal inhibition will continuously reset active areas to enable the constant monitoring of information flow from the environment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional role of inhibition.

claim: Without inhibition, response enhancement will not be possible since tectal output cells rapidly saturate.
source: Without this inhibition, response enhancement will not be possible since tectal output cells rapidly saturate most likely due to a ceiling effect, making neurons incapable of further responding and thereby losing their response sensitivity, and hence, event detection reliability.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the gabazine experiments showing loss of enhancement.

claim: Tectal inhibitory action can be interpreted as a gain modulatory mechanism.
source: Tectal inhibitory action can be interpreted as a gain modulatory mechanism whose effects are well captured by the conductance-based analysis of output neurons, and visible throughout a wide range of membrane potentials (i.e., varying from below to above spike threshold).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the inhibitory mechanism based on the conductance analysis.

claim: Local circuit dynamics triggered by sensory inputs allow depolarizing synaptic events to reach the reversal potential of the synaptic response.
source: Local circuit dynamics triggered by sensory inputs will allow for depolarizing synaptic events to reach the reversal potential of the synaptic response.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the conductance analysis.

claim: The reversal potential value is invariant during unimodal or bimodal stimulation.
source: We show that this value is invariant during unimodal or bimodal stimulation
evidence: This is a primary finding from the conductance analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A strong unimodal stimulus can bring the membrane potential to action potential threshold, as well as two weaker bimodal stimuli.
source: implying that a strong unimodal stimulus can bring the membrane potential to action potential threshold, as well as two weaker bimodal stimuli.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the invariant reversal potential finding.

claim: When bimodal stimuli overlap, they reinforce each other and generate larger depolarizing currents that increase the likelihood that output neurons reach spike threshold before inhibition fully develops.
source: When bimodal stimuli overlap, they will reinforce each other and generate larger depolarizing currents that will increase the likelihood that the output neurons reach spike threshold before inhibition fully develops.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the temporal integration experiments.

claim: Enhancement most likely arises from sensory inputs that target different dendritic compartments of output neurons that were previously inactive during unimodal stimulation.
source: This enhancement most likely arises from sensory inputs that target the different dendritic compartments of output neurons (i.e., superficial vs intermediate layer), that were previously inactive during unimodal stimulation.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of enhancement based on the morphology and layer-specific inputs.

claim: Tectum can perform stimulus selection without external control from any other brain region.
source: Although our findings imply that tectum can perform stimulus selection without the external control from any other brain region
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study showing local circuits are sufficient for multisensory integration.

claim: Activity in the deep layer output neurons can be strongly influenced by forebrain structures such as the cortex and the basal ganglia.
source: activity in the deep layer output neurons can be strongly influenced by forebrain structures such as the cortex and the basal ganglia.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about tectal connectivity.

claim: Tectal output neurons receive the combination of inhibitory and excitatory input from the forebrain in both lamprey and mammals.
source: As in mammals, tectal output neurons in lamprey also receive the combination of inhibitory and excitatory input from the forebrain.
evidence: This statement draws from comparative neuroanatomy.

claim: GABAergic output neurons of the basal ganglia provide tonic inhibition at rest in both lamprey and primates.
source: The GABAergic output neurons of the basal ganglia output nuclei provide tonic inhibition at rest in both lamprey and primates, and can trigger movements by way of disinhibition of the tectal output neurons (Wurtz and Hikosaka, 1986; Stephenson-Jones et al., 2012; Kim and Hikosaka, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pallium projects to the lamprey optic tectum and provides monosynaptic excitation to the output neurons in the deep layer.
source: Pallium (evolutionary forerunner of the mammalian cortex) projects to the lamprey optic tectum and provides monosynaptic excitation to the output neurons in the deep layer, and its stimulation is able to elicit eye-head gaze movements (Ocaña et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Basal ganglia disinhibition is likely complementary to the excitation conveyed from pallium/cortex.
source: In the forebrain control of tectum, it would seem likely that the basal ganglia disinhibition will be complementary to the excitation conveyed from pallium/cortex
evidence: This is speculation about the interaction between different forebrain inputs.

claim: Forebrain inputs target the soma level of the output neurons rather than the dendrites.
source: and in both cases they target the soma level of the output neurons rather than the dendrites.
evidence: This statement draws from anatomical knowledge.

claim: Extracellular recordings in cats and primates have shown a supra-linear enhancement of deep layer collicular activity in response to overlapping weak multimodal stimuli.
source: Extracellular recordings in cats and primates have shown a supra-linear enhancement of deep layer collicular activity in response to overlapping weak multimodal stimuli (Meredith and Stein, 1983; Wallace and Stein, 1994; Wallace et al., 1996; Stein, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Supra-linear amplification is thought not to arise from the intrinsic collicular circuitry, but from extrinsic cortico-collicular afferents from the anterior ectosylvian sulcus.
source: This amplification is thought not to arise from the intrinsic collicular circuitry, but from extrinsic cortico-collicular afferents from the anterior ectosylvian sulcus.
evidence: This statement refers to a hypothesis from prior research.

claim: When the anterior ectosylvian sulcus is inactivated, the amplification vanishes.
source: When this area is inactivated the amplification vanishes (Wallace and Stein, 1994; Jiang et al., 2001; Alvarado et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: One mechanism for supra-linear enhancement would be to bypass tectal inhibition by selectively increasing excitation onto the output neurons.
source: One mechanism would be to bypass tectal inhibition by selectively increasing excitation onto the output neurons, which are targeted by monosynaptic projections from cortex/pallium in both mammals and lamprey.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms for cortical modulation.

claim: Another potential mechanism for introducing non-linearities could be a selective decrease of inhibition by briefly 'switching off' the tectal GABAergic system.
source: Another potential mechanism that would introduce such non-linearities could be a selective decrease of inhibition by briefly 'switching off' the tectal GABAergic system.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms for cortical modulation.

claim: Variable classes of tectal interneurons may provide additional flexibility to manipulate sensorimotor processing within the optic tectum.
source: The variable classes of tectal interneurons may also provide an additional flexibility to manipulate sensorimotor processing within the optic tectum.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed diversity of interneuron response patterns.

claim: The basic anatomical and functional organization of the optic tectum across vertebrates is highly conserved from the lamprey.
source: The basic anatomical and functional organization of the optic tectum across vertebrates is highly conserved, from the earliest group of vertebrates that has evolved - the lamprey (Nieuwenhuys and Nicholson, 1998; Saitoh et al., 2007; Jones et al., 2009; Asteriti et al., 2015; Kardamakis et al., 2015)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to comparative neuroanatomy studies.

claim: The lamprey optic tectum consists of glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons activated by unimodal and bimodal inputs.
source: The lamprey optic tectum consists of glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons activated by unimodal and bimodal inputs.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Output neurons found in the deep layer are excitatory and project to the brainstem, and control gaze movements.
source: The output neurons found in the deep layer are excitatory and project to the brainstem, and control gaze movements (Saitoh et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In lamprey, visual and electrosensory stimuli evoke direct excitation quickly followed by recruited inhibition onto output neurons.
source: In lamprey, visual and electrosensory stimuli evoke direct excitation quickly followed by recruited inhibition onto these output neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Synaptic responses are amplified when spatiotemporally aligned bimodal inputs are present, leading to response enhancement.
source: These synaptic responses are amplified when spatiotemporally aligned bimodal inputs are present, thus, leading to a response enhancement.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Sensory-evoked inhibition scales the neural activity of output cells to allow for robust spatiotemporal integration.
source: We have shown here that sensory-evoked inhibition scales the neural activity of output cells to allow for a robust spatiotemporal integration, capable of integrating the enormous amount of incoming sensory inputs during natural conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: Local inhibition may be critical for spatiotemporal processing not only in lamprey but also in other vertebrates.
source: Local inhibition may be critical for spatiotemporal processing not only in lamprey but also in other vertebrates.
evidence: This is speculation based on the conserved organization of the optic tectum across vertebrates.

claim: Experiments were performed on 47 adult river lampreys (Lampetra fluviatilis).
source: Experiments were performed on 47 adult river lampreys (Lampetra fluviatilis).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the study.
